books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — Roosevelt as 'Trust Buster'
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20; verbatim excerpt (abridged) from Theodore Roosevelt's 1903 speech, public domain.
stimulus.text:
Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20: In 1902, anthracite coal miners went on strike, and President Theodore Roosevelt called both sides to the White House, threatening to take over the mines if the owners would not negotiate. The miners won a 10 percent wage increase but not union recognition. Roosevelt called the settlement a 'Square Deal.' He also used the Sherman Antitrust Act against the Northern Securities Company, a railroad holding company, and in 1904 the Supreme Court upheld the breakup.

'We must act upon the motto of all for each and each for all. ... We must see that each is given a square deal, because he is entitled to no more and should receive no less.' — Theodore Roosevelt, speech to farmers in New York, 1903 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: Roosevelt's suit against the Northern Securities Company best illustrates his view that

options.text: all large companies must be destroyed by the federal government
options.misconception: Roosevelt distinguished good trusts from bad ones; he did not aim to destroy every large company.

options.text: railroads should be left completely alone by the federal government
options.misconception: Roosevelt sued a railroad holding company; leaving railroads alone was the opposite of his action.

options.text: the Sherman Antitrust Act was unconstitutional and unenforceable
options.misconception: Roosevelt used the Sherman Act and won in the Supreme Court; he relied on it, he did not attack it.

options.text: the government should break up only trusts that restrained trade

rationales.A: Roosevelt left large companies he judged well-behaved alone. His target was not bigness but restraint of trade.
rationales.B: Suing a railroad holding company is the opposite of leaving railroads alone.
rationales.C: Roosevelt's case rested on the Sherman Act, and the Court upheld it in 1904. He trusted the act, not attacked it.
rationales.D: Northern Securities controlled the railroads of the Northwest and had eliminated competition there. Roosevelt sued that combination because it restrained trade, while leaving large companies he judged well-behaved alone.
rationales.general:
1. Name the target. Northern Securities was a holding company controlling the Northwest's railroads and killing competition.
2. Name the rule. Roosevelt pursued bad trusts, combinations that restrained trade, not bigness itself.
3. Rule out the extremes. He neither destroyed all big business nor left railroads alone.
Remember: Roosevelt's trust policy was a judgment, not a slogan, so ask what the trust did before deciding why he sued.
